p.title: The Effects of Firms' Lobbying on Resource Misallocation

ext.title: The Effects of Firms' Lobbying on Resource Misallocation
ext.venue: SSRN working paper (SSRN 3275097); first draft Oct 29, 2018, this draft Nov 12, 2018. No journal publication stated.
ext.coverage: Full text read: all 12,431 lines of the extracted PDF text (abstract, Sections 1-5, Appendices A-F, references, figure and table text). Lines 1-1,999 read raw. Lines 2,000 onward were read from a scratchpad copy with only figure plot-marker lines (lines made solely of the token G) removed; no prose or table content was dropped. All 68 Paul Goff annotations were read from _annots/a18804866401.json (the only annotation file for this paper). Annotation page = PDF page index; printed pages below are the paper's own numbering (annotation page = printed page + 1). Metadata hint corrected: authors and SSRN 3275097 are correct; the work is an SSRN working paper dated 2018.
ext.research_question: Does firms' lobbying causally increase firm size, and how much does lobbying reduce aggregate productivity through misallocation of resources across firms (distortion of firm size)? (Abstract; Introduction, printed pp.1-3)
ext.theory: Heterogeneous-firm general-equilibrium model with endogenous lobbying, extending Hsieh and Klenow (2009) along Melitz (2003) lines. Firms differ in productivity, lobbying productivity and an exogenous wedge; a fixed lobbying cost induces selection into lobbying; lobbying yields output distortions tau_s(phi) that raise a lobbying firm's revenue (eq. 1, p.14). Microfoundation (Section 3.2, pp.18-20): a three-stage game in which the government's welfare combines household utility with a CES aggregate of lobbying expenditure (a generalization of Grossman and Helpman 1994). Stated rationale for heterogeneous distortions: the government's "love for variety" in lobbying reduces political risk from concentrated influence (p.20). Proposition 3 (p.20): distortions rise with the mass of lobbying firms and fall with the lobbying elasticity sigma_L.
ext.data: Lobbying: parsed LD-1 and LD-2 Lobbying Disclosure Act reports from the Senate Office of Public Records, 1999-2015 filings (Appendix A, printed p.38); 972,005 report-level observations after dropping amendments. More than one million original filings were parsed (p.4). Client names linked to Compustat gvkeys: 67,842 unique client names (p.5). Bills and committees: 65,047 lobbied bills across the 106th-115th Congresses (Figure 5; the 1,862 trade bills are a subset); committee assignments from Stewart and Woon (2011). Firm sample: all US publicly traded firms in Compustat, 1999-2018 (p.4-5). Unit: firm-year (Table 2 regressions). Regression N for log sales: 15,332 (all years) and 8,796 (post-2007); profits: 10,369 and 6,064; value added (Table F.2): 10,851 and 6,097. Industry data: BEA value-added, labor, and intermediate input shares for 2000-2017 (Figures 8-11). Campaign contributions: FEC data (Figure 1). Financial variables are described only as standard characteristics of public firms (the source database is not named in the extracted text).
ext.method: Descriptive stylized facts (Section 2); OLS and IV panel regressions of log sales and log profits on log lobbying expenditure with firm, year and state-year fixed effects, standard errors double-clustered by firm and year (Table 2, Appendix F); structural model estimated by simulated method of moments (nine parameters: production and lobbying fixed costs, variances and covariances of productivity and wedge, and beta), with sigma_C=4, death rate 0.025 and beta_s=beta imposed (pp.27-31); counterfactual with beta=0 and a sensitivity sweep over sigma_C (pp.31-32). The SMM text says the weighting matrix is the generalized inverse of the moment covariance, but for now it uses the identity matrix (fn.22, p.29).
ext.identification: Shift-share instrument (eq. 12, p.21): z_it = sum over politicians j in firm i's connections of [sum over committees c of w_ict-k * d_jct]. Share w_ict-k = firm i's share of lobbied bills assigned to committee c, lagged (preferred t-1; t-2 and t-3 in Tables F.1-F.2). Shift d_jct = indicator that politician j sits on committee c in year t. Connections = politicians representing the state of the firm's headquarters. Identifying assumption: committee moves by politicians are exogenous to firm characteristics and influence (p.22). Relevance: 30 percent average probability a politician changes committee between Congresses (p.22; about 29 percent in Figure C.2).
ext.scope: Population: US publicly traded firms in Compustat (1999-2018) and lobbying clients of federal lobbying disclosure filings. Institution: US federal lobbying under the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995 and congressional standing committees (Table C.2; Figure 6 and C.1 show senators, 106th-115th Congresses). Era: 1999-2018. Model economy: multi-industry US economy with 17 industries (Figures 8-11).

key_findings.finding: Lobbying is rare: only 766 of 7,646 public US firms lobbied in 2017; average share of public firms lobbying across years is 11.8 percent (text figure; 766/7,646 is about 10.0 percent for 2017 alone).
key_findings.numbers: 766 of 7,646 firms (2017); 11.8 percent average; manufacturing 15.8 percent lobby, 6.5 percent in-house

key_findings.finding: Lobbying spending exceeds campaign contributions: on average lobbying is more than six times larger than campaign contributions (PAC, party, candidate and other federal committee contributions; individual contributions excluded).
key_findings.numbers: more than 6x on average (2 year cycles, 1999-2016)

key_findings.finding: Firm size and lobbying are positively correlated on the intensive margin (conditional on lobbying).
key_findings.numbers: log lobbying coefficient on log sales = 0.984 (p=0.000, t=28.13)

key_findings.finding: Lobbying is highly persistent. More than 80 percent of firms that lobbied in 2016 lobbied in 2017; the intensive-margin correlation of log lobbying across adjacent years is high, though persistence dropped during 2007-2009.
Firm-level lobbying exceeds lobbying by business and industry organizations (figure only; no dollar totals stated in the text).
Most congressional bills are lobbied by only one or two interest groups (narrow, firm-specific lobbying).
key_findings.location: Fact 6, Figure 5, Table C.1, printed pp.11-12
key_findings.numbers: median 2 clients per bill; mean 3.45 clients across 65,047 bills; trade bills: 1,862 bills, mean 3.21, median 2

key_findings.finding: Headline causal result: a 10 percent increase in lobbying expenditure raises revenue by about 3 percent (IV). The text also reports IV estimates are an order of magnitude above OLS; Table 2 shows IV is about 4.5 to 7 times OLS.
key_findings.location: Abstract; Introduction printed p.2; Table 2 printed p.26
key_findings.numbers: Table 2 log sales: OLS 0.0436 (all) and 0.0500 (post-2007); IV 0.319 (all, SE 0.0754, first-stage F 14.30) and 0.227 (post-2007, SE 0.0795, F 13.10)

key_findings.finding: Internal inconsistency: the 3 percent headline matches the full-sample IV coefficient (0.319); the text calls post-2007 column 4 (0.227, implying about 2.3 percent per 10 percent) the preferred estimate and says 1 percent lobbying gives 0.2 percent revenue.
Profit results mirror sales: IV profit coefficients are positive and larger than OLS, though only the post-2007 IV is significant at the 10 percent level.
key_findings.numbers: OLS profits 0.0241 (all), 0.0468 (post-2007); IV profits 0.322 (all, SE 0.114), 0.236 (post-2007, SE 0.124)

key_findings.finding: Robustness to lagged weights and value added: IV sales coefficients stay positive with t-2 and t-3 weights, but first-stage F falls (t-3 all-sample F = 6.0). Value-added IV coefficients are 0.287 (all) and 0.177 (post-2007) with t-1 weights.
key_findings.location: Appendix F, Tables F.1-F.2, printed pp.10-12

key_findings.finding: Calibrated model: the estimated model reproduces the targeted moments approximately. Targeted IV 1-beta is 0.23 in the data and 0.19 in the model (implying beta = 0.81); OLS 1-beta is 0.05 in the data and 0.045 in the model. Other targeted moments are listed in Table 3.
key_findings.numbers: data/model: v(phi_P) 2.8/2.4; v(phi_L) 2.1/1.8; v(phi_tau) 1.1/1.6; corr(phi_P,phi_L) 0.5/0.3; corr(phi_P,phi_tau) -0.5/-0.1; corr(phi_L,phi_tau) 0.2/0.4; 1-beta IV 0.23/0.19; 1-beta OLS 0.05/0.045

key_findings.finding: Counterfactual with no return to lobbying (beta=0): aggregate productivity would be 22 percent higher than under the estimated return. About 41 percent of that loss comes through the entry channel (lower wages make entry cheaper); the rest comes from misallocation among incumbents.
key_findings.location: Counterfactual, printed pp.31-32; Conclusion printed p.33
key_findings.numbers: 22 percent productivity loss; 41 percent via entry

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity to the elasticity of substitution sigma_C (set to 4): the loss is about 38 percent at sigma_C=2 and about 13 percent at sigma_C=6.

limitations: Identification depends on committee-membership moves being exogenous to firms. The authors concede politicians may choose committees to deliver targeted benefits to connected firms (printed p.26) and that committee weights could reflect anticipated changes (tested with a near-zero correlation, p.25).
Headquarters are assumed fixed; the authors report no headquarter changes in their data, and a politician changing district has under 1 percent probability (p.24-25).
The instrument's relevance is modest: first-stage F is 13-14 in the preferred specifications and falls to 6-10 with t-2 or t-3 weights (Tables 2, F.1, F.2).
Headline 3 percent versus preferred-column 0.2 percent inconsistency (see key findings); the text's claim of an order-of-magnitude IV-OLS gap does not match Table 2 (about 4.5 to 7 times).

Elasticity of substitution sigma_C is not estimated; it is fixed at 4 for lack of data, and the paper acknowledges results depend on it (p.27, p.32). Industry-specific beta_s and sigma_C are restricted to be common across industries (p.27).

Model is simplified: one industry and one factor for exposition (fn.14); demand shifters ignored (fn.9); extensions to decreasing returns and demand shifters deferred to future versions (fn.10); Hsieh-Klenow caveats (Haltiwanger et al. 2018) noted but not addressed; the counterfactual uses aggregate productivity, not output, because there is no capital or human capital accumulation (fn.23). The analysis is partial equilibrium except for the Section 4.2 general-equilibrium counterfactual (fn.13).

Lobbying-to-distortion mapping is assumed in Section 3.1 and microfounded only through a government welfare function whose lobbying-income motive is not justified (p.19-20, fn.15). Equation (10) assumes truth-telling, and coordination issues are set aside as beyond scope (p.19).
SMM uses an identity weighting matrix for the baseline, despite the stated generalized-inverse weighting (fn.22, p.29).

Lobbying amounts are self-reported estimates rounded to the nearest $5,000 (pre-2008 larger rounding bins; Appendix A, fn.25). Client-name matching is algorithmic plus manual, validated on a 5 percent random sample (Appendix A, fn.27-28, printed p.38-39).
Date inconsistency: the data are described as covering 1999-2018 (Introduction), but Appendix A says LD-1 and LD-2 filings from 1999-2015 were used.
The persistence measure is conservative (two adjacent years only), and the persistence drops during the 2007-2009 crisis (p.10).
Open questions the authors leave: why entry into lobbying is limited, why persistence is high, the reverse effect of size on lobbying, and business-cycle effects (p.33).

rel.summary_md:
Huneeus and Kim link federal LDA lobbying reports (1999-2015 filings, about 972k report rows) to US public firms in Compustat. They ask two questions: does lobbying make a firm bigger, and what does that cost the economy in productivity?

**Descriptive facts**
- Lobbying is rare: 766 of 7,646 public firms lobbied in 2017.
- It is very persistent: more than 80% of 2016 lobbyists lobbied again in 2017, with an intensive-margin slope of 0.922.
- It runs to more than 6 times PAC-type campaign contributions.
- Most bills draw a median of 2 lobbying clients.

**Causal estimate.** The instrument is a shift-share. For each firm it combines its lagged share of lobbied bills going to each committee with the committee seats held by politicians from its headquarters state. The IV elasticity of sales on lobbying is 0.319 for all years (first-stage F 14.3) and 0.227 after 2007 (F 13.1). OLS gives about 0.04-0.05. The paper's "3 percent per 10 percent" headline uses the full-sample estimate, while its stated preferred estimate is 0.2 percent per 1 percent.

**Structural model.** A Hsieh-Klenow/Melitz model is fitted by SMM with an identity weighting matrix. With sigma_C fixed at 4, removing the return to lobbying raises aggregate productivity by 22%. That figure moves from 38% to 13% as sigma_C goes from 2 to 6.

**What it means for Paul's systems.** Nothing here estimates how a member of Congress responds to money. The usable pieces are narrower:
- The committee-relevance weight is computed from data, where the committee pillar's tier weights are owner judgment.
- The persistence facts explain why naive carry-forward is hard to beat in Mentat's lobbying forecasts.
- The paper's causal direction (lobbying leads to revenue) is a simultaneity warning for the sector-growth study's growth-leads-to-lobbying regressions.
- Appendix A's fuzzy matching with a 5% random validation sample is a template for auditing the LDA client classifier.

All transfers are UNVERIFIED (DE-062) until a second path reproduces them.

bearings.paper_claim: Lobbying causally raises firm revenue. IV log-sales elasticity is 0.319 (all years, SE 0.0754, first-stage F 14.30) and 0.227 (post-2007, F 13.10), against OLS of 0.0436 and 0.0500, with firm, year and state-year fixed effects (sample: Compustat public firms, firm-years, N=15,332 and 8,796). The reverse effect of size on lobbying is left as an open question. Lobbying persistence fell during 2007-2009.
bearings.paper_location: Table 2, printed p.26; Conclusion p.33; Fact 4 p.10
bearings.system_side: The L-LV family regresses log sector lobbying (LobbyView, de-duplicated) on lagged sector growth with an AR term. The R-yearFE robustness variant swaps national controls for sector and year fixed effects, and the recorded result is that the lobbying lead flips sign under year FE. Lobbying series are LDA outside-firm income, self-filer expenses and the LobbyView undifferentiated amount.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over as a design warning: if lobbying feeds revenue, then a growth-to-lobbying regression has simultaneity, and OLS with fixed effects cannot sign it. H&K's IV is 4.5 to 7 times OLS, which is consistent with attenuated or biased OLS in the same family of data. It does not carry over as an effect size. H&K work at firm level on public firms only, with federal LDA filings from 1999-2015 and no trade associations. The SGS works on sector-year aggregates that include associations. Their instrument needs headquarters state and bill-to-committee shares per firm, and the sector panel has neither. H&K do not say how they handle self-filer and outside-firm double counting, which the SGS de-duplicates (a median 9-26% by sector), so their dollar series is not directly comparable.

bearings.paper_claim: Firm lobbying is highly persistent. More than 80% of firms that lobbied in 2016 also lobbied in 2017, and the adjacent-year log-lobbying slope is 0.922 (t=157.88, conditional on lobbying in both years). Persistence dropped during 2007-2009.
bearings.system_side: The lobbying console rule is last year's level plus slope times the change in growth, backtested on rolling origins with 2014-2023 targets. Gate G9 warns when a refit fails to beat naive. The recorded log-lobbying MAE is 4.050 against naive 3.936.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Near-unit persistence at firm level makes a carry-forward naive forecast a strong baseline, so losing to naive is the expected result rather than a defect. Sector aggregates should be smoother still. The evidence is federal LDA 1999-2015. The 2007-2009 break is outside the 2014-2023 target window, so regime shifts like that one are not in the backtest. Persistence says nothing about whether growth adds signal.

bearings.paper_claim: Committee relevance is measured from data. w_ict-k is the firm's share of lobbied bills referred to committee c, lagged (t-1 preferred; t-2 and t-3 in robustness). Interacted with committee seats held by connected politicians, it gives a first-stage F of 13-14. About 30% of politicians change committee between Congresses.
bearings.paper_location: Eq. 12 p.21; p.22; Figure C.2; Tables F.1-F.2
bearings.system_side: Seat relevance is an owner-judged tier: Highly 3.0, Moderately 1.8, Slightly 0.9. Subcommittee seats count 1/6, and leadership multipliers are KLEAD. No weight comes from where CU bills are actually referred.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The extension is to compute each committee's share of CU-category bills referred to it, lagged one Congress, and compare it with the tier labels. The referrals must come from congress.gov billstatus, not LDA lobbied-bill lists, because D-021 makes LDA an identity source and not a weight source. H&K's weights are specific to each firm and validated only as an instrument for firm revenue. They give no evidence that referral-share weights predict a member's CU effectiveness, so any re-weighting needs its own look.

bearings.paper_claim: LDA client names (61,478 unique) were matched to Compustat with FuzzyWuzzy, then Bureau van Dijk ISIN and ticker lookup, then the CRP standardized client name, then manual checks. Precision was checked on a 5% random sample of client names. Messy spellings and abbreviations are named as the main hazard.
bearings.system_side: Bank, CU or other is assigned by name regex with guards (CREDIT_UNION_RE, association patterns such as NAFCU and CUNA Mutual). NAICS is linkage metadata only and the rules fail closed. No random-sample precision audit is recorded.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The transferable piece is the 5% random-sample validation protocol, not the fuzzy matcher. The project's never-guess and strict-names rules reject fuzzy acceptance. H&K's target set is public firms, but most CUs are not in Compustat and CU lobbying runs mainly through associations such as CUNA and NAFCU, which H&K's firm match leaves out. So their match rates and Fact 5 (firm lobbying exceeds association lobbying) do not carry over to the CU side.

bearings.paper_claim: The return to lobbying is measured as firm revenue (elasticity 0.227-0.319), not as member votes or positions. Lobbying spend is more than 6 times PAC, party and candidate contributions (2-year cycles, 1999-2016, individual contributions excluded).
bearings.system_side: pflip combines saturating money terms for CU and industry dollars (from FEC receipts in congestion.json, with industry = banks + finserv PAC money) with peer proximity, at WM 0.35 and WP 0.65. No lobbying spend enters.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Paul lists H&K as support for the flip model, but the paper has no member-level outcome, so it cannot calibrate WM, HALFF or the saturation. Its only relevance is the scale fact: the largest corporate political channel (lobbying) is absent from the money terms. That gap is deliberate under D-021, which keeps LDA out of edges and weights, so this is not a recommendation to add LDA dollars.

bearings.paper_claim: Firm-politician 'connection' is defined as the politicians representing the firm's headquarters state. The paper reports no headquarters moves in its data and under a 1% chance of a politician changing district. The instrument built on this home-state link has first-stage F of about 13-14.
bearings.system_side: Footprint v3.0 (the default) scores districts by CU employment LQ (.30), establishment LQ (.20), branch share (.25) and deposit share (.25). It qualifies a district at employment LQ >= 1.0. It does not feed Demo%.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Gives weak support to Paul's state-layer idea that a constituency's industry presence links it to its representatives. But in H&K the link is an identifying assumption at state level for headquarters only, not an estimated effect of employment or branch footprint, and it is not district level. It does not validate the footprint weights or any claim that footprint predicts CU-aligned behaviour.

gaps_exposed: Committee relevance tiers are owner judgment. The system has no data-derived check of where CU-category bills are actually referred, lagged by Congress, which is the committee weight H&K build. Any version must use congress.gov referrals, not LDA (D-021).
The LDA finance-client classifier has no recorded random-sample precision audit like H&K's 5% client-name validation.

The sector-growth study is all OLS or fixed effects with no exogenous variation. H&K show lobbying feeding revenue, so the system has no way to separate growth driving lobbying from lobbying driving growth.
No company-level lobbying panel exists in Mentat linking roster companies' LDA spend to their own performance. All lobbying analysis is sector aggregate.

Firm versus association lobbying is not split for the CU sector. H&K's firm-dominance fact (Fact 5) is for public firms and probably inverts for CUs, which lobby mainly through associations; this has not been measured.
flags: Headline inconsistency: '3 percent per 10 percent' is the full-sample IV (0.319), but the authors' stated preferred column (post-2007, 0.227) gives about 0.2 percent per 1 percent. Paul highlighted both. Any quote must name the window (all years versus post-2007, Compustat public firms, federal LDA 1999-2015 filings) and the column.

The 22% productivity loss depends on the model. It comes from a fixed sigma_C=4 (13-38% across sigma_C 2-6), SMM with an identity weighting matrix, and an industry-common beta. Never quote it as a measured quantity.
The Table 2 coefficients are pooled across all industries, with beta_s restricted to be equal across industries. Quoting them for finance or CU lobbying requires an UNSTRATIFIED label.
D-021: neither the committee-weight extension nor the flip-model scale gap may be implemented with LDA as an edge or weight source.

Paul's positions cite H&K under the flip model, joint optimizer, workbook allocator, break-even and ROI, cycle model and employer match. The paper has no member-level or allocation evidence, so those citations do not carry over as support. The system's own sector-growth study (no stable growth effect) is the closer test.
The instrument rests on committee assignment being exogenous to firms, and the authors concede that it may not be (p.26). Treat the causal claim as moderate (F 13-14, and 6-10 with deeper lags).
Every bearing here is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's annotation record for this work is empty: no takeaways and no system links. His highlights focus on the identification strategy (headquarters-state connections and committee moves), the 3% and 22% headline numbers, and the Appendix A client-name matching. The evidence matches his committee-pillar reading (lobbying value runs through committee position) and gives weak support to his state-layer and footprint idea. It does not support using H&K to set fundraising goals, price member flips or justify ROI. The paper measures firm revenue returns to lobbying, not legislator responses to PAC dollars. Several of his positions are stale relative to the system now. The sector-growth study found no stable growth effect, and its lobbying lead flips sign under year fixed effects, which cuts against a confident ROI reading. The flip model deliberately excludes LDA dollars (D-021). The highlight inconsistency between 3% and 0.2% is the paper's own, and Paul highlighted both without noting the conflict.

related.why: LobbyView is the firm-name-disambiguated LDA and bill database this paper builds on and releases. The system's collect_lobbyview.py ingests it.
Same LobbyView firm linkage, joined to FEC donations. It addresses the PAC-lobbying relation behind H&K's Fact 2 (lobbying more than 6 times contributions).
Uses the same bill-level LobbyView data that H&K use to compute committee shares and clients per bill (median 2).
A survey of empirical lobbying models, including returns-to-lobbying designs like H&K's IV and the Grossman-Helpman microfoundation.
Links corporate lobbying and PACs to market concentration, the same resource-misallocation story at industry level.
A single-policy lobbying ROI estimate that Paul calls an outlier. H&K's 0.2-0.3 revenue elasticity is the economy-wide counterpart.
Its two-way fixed-effects caution applies to H&K's OLS columns and to the system's sector-growth regressions.
Finds low overlap between organizational lobbying and PAC spending, which qualifies any use of H&K's lobbying-to-contribution ratio.
Models committee assignment as a matching process. That bears directly on H&K's identifying assumption that committee moves are exogenous to firms.
Committee structure in the House. H&K's committee-share weights treat committees as the channel through which lobbying is valued.

paul_entries.text:
Huneeus, Federico, and In Song Kim. “The effects of firms’ lobbying on Resource Misallocation.” *SSRN Electronic Journal*, 12 Nov. 2018, [https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3275097](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3275097).

This article by Massachusetts Institute of Technology Professor In Song Kim, and Princeton Professor Federico Huneeus examines the optimization, and more specifically mis-allocation, of company revenue on political lobbying. The main finding is that a 10% increase in lobbying expenditures leads to a 3% gain in revenue. Additionally, the article introduces a novel methodology used to capture this finding, using the general equilibrium firm model that features endogenous variables. The fundamental application of this paper to the present research is being able to set fundraising goals, and use the current models as a basis to help inform the appropriate amount for future targets and institutions. However, there are several gaps within the literature as they pertain to the present research. First, is that the model does not distinguish campaign donations from events, meetings, etc. Second, is that the models make no differentiation between the representatives, however its state layer can shed insight as to who should be targeted based on general industry presence. In all, Professor Kim delivers another key step into the optimization and empirical application of mathematical models and principals to the realm of political advocacy, serving as the basis for business-applicable models.

“*We find that a 10 percent increase in lobbying expenditure leads to a 3 percent gain in revenue.*” This article examines both the macro and micro-level effects of company spending on lobbying, showing a robust increase in individual company revenue, if at the expense of the broader market production, not industry-specific, but broader economy as a whole.
